title: Does non-symbolic and symbolic representation depend on visual-spatial working memory across school education?
abstract: Context and relevance. Representation of quantitative information is an integral component of understanding the world around us and underlies academic success in STEM disciplines. At the same time, the accuracy of quantitative perception presented in various formats is dependent to varying degrees on visual-spatial working memory throughout school education, and both are considered a “double deficit” of cognitive resources in learning. Objective: to study the specifics of the dependence of the accuracy of both non-symbolic and symbolic representation on visual-spatial working memory in schoolchildren at the primary (grades 4) and secondary (grades 9) school. Methods and materials. The study involved 1,013 schoolchildren, including 511 fourth-grade students (Mage = 10.7, SD = 0.5; 49.2% girls) and 502 ninth-grade students (Mage = 15.9, SD = 0.5; 52.2% girls). The non-symbolic and symbolic representations were used by “Number Sense” and the “Number Line” tests, respectively (Tikhomirova, Malykh, 2022). Visual-spatial working memory was assessed using the “Corsi Block Test” (Tikhomirova, 2025). Results. The accuracy of non-symbolic representation is moderately and directly proportional to visual-spatial working memory; and this relationship is observed at both primary and secondary school, with a significant increase at the end of schooling. The accuracy of symbolic representation is less dependent on working memory and is observed only at the primary school. Conclusions. The dependence of the accuracy of non-symbolic and symbolic representations on visual-spatial working memory is mediated by the format of quantity presentation and has a pronounced age-related character.
